claim: Paired recordings between hippocampal CA1 pyramidal cells and fast-spiking interneurons in acute slices from adult mice demonstrate large variability in the number of release sites (N) at these connections.
source: Paired recordings between hippocampal CA1 pyramidal cells and fast-spiking interneurons in acute slices from adult mice followed by quantal analysis demonstrate large variability in the number of RSs (N) at these connections.
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental paired recordings followed by quantal analysis that directly measured variability in N.

claim: High-resolution molecular analysis of functionally characterized synapses reveals variability in the content of Munc13-1 in active zones that possess the same N.
source: High-resolution molecular analysis of functionally characterized synapses reveals variability in the content of one of the key vesicle priming factors – Munc13-1 – in AZs that possess the same N.
evidence: The manuscript describes high-resolution molecular analysis performed on functionally characterized synapses showing Munc13-1 variability.

claim: Replica immunolabeling shows a threefold variability in the total Munc13-1 content of active zones of identical size.
source: Replica immunolabeling also shows a threefold variability in the total Munc13-1 content of AZs of identical size and a fourfold variability in the size and density of Munc13-1 clusters within the AZs.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative measurements from replica immunolabeling experiments.

claim: Replica immunolabeling shows a fourfold variability in the size and density of Munc13-1 clusters within active zones.
source: Replica immunolabeling also shows a threefold variability in the total Munc13-1 content of AZs of identical size and a fourfold variability in the size and density of Munc13-1 clusters within the AZs.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative measurements from replica immunolabeling experiments.

claim: The active zone is built up from variable numbers of molecularly heterogeneous, but independent release sites.
source: Our results provide evidence for quantitative molecular heterogeneity of RSs and support a model in which the AZ is built up from variable numbers of molecularly heterogeneous, but independent RSs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Different types of central neurons form synapses with widely different structures, molecular compositions, and functional properties.
source: It has been known for decades that different types of central neurons form synapses with widely different structures, molecular compositions, and functional properties, resulting in large variations in the amplitude and kinetics of the postsynaptic responses and the type of short- and long-term plasticity.
evidence: This statement references established knowledge in the field ('known for decades').

claim: Different pre- and postsynaptic molecule isoforms underlie functional variability among synapses made by distinct pre- and postsynaptic cell types.
source: When the mechanisms underlying distinct functions were investigated among synapses made by distinct pre- and postsynaptic cell types (e.g. hippocampal mossy fiber vs. Schaffer collateral vs. calyx of Held vs. cerebellar climbing fiber etc. synapses), most studies converged to the conclusion that different pre- (e.g. different types of Ca channels, Ca sensors) and postsynaptic (e.g. different types of AMPA receptor subunits) molecule isoforms underlie the functional variability (reviewed by Südhof, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review by Südhof, 2012.

claim: Postsynaptic target cell type-dependent variability in vesicle release probability and short-term plasticity was identified in cortical and hippocampal networks.
source: Such postsynaptic target cell type-dependent variability in vesicle release probability (Pv) and short-term plasticity was identified in cortical and hippocampal networks (Koester and Johnston, 2005; Losonczy et al., 2002; Pouille and Scanziani, 2004; Reyes et al., 1998; Rozov et al., 2001; Scanziani et al., 1998; Thomson, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: Different molecules and variable densities of the same molecules were suggested as key molecular features underlying postsynaptic target cell type-dependent variability.
source: Studies investigating the underlying mechanisms revealed not only different molecules (e.g. mGluR7, kainate receptors in the AZ and Elfn1 in the postsynaptic density [PSD], Shigemoto et al., 1996; Sylwestrak and Ghosh, 2012), but variable densities of the same molecules were also suggested as key molecular features (Éltes et al., 2017; Rozov et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: There is large structural and functional diversity of synapses established by molecularly identical pre- and postsynaptic neuron types.
source: Probably even more surprising is the large structural and functional diversity of synapses that are established by molecularly identical pre- and postsynaptic neuron types (e.g. synapses among cerebellar molecular layer interneurons [INs], Pulido et al., 2015; among hippocampal CA3, Holderith et al., 2012), suggesting that qualitative molecular differences are unlikely to be responsible for the functional diversity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The number of functional release sites varied from 1 to 6 per active zone in cerebellar molecular layer interneuron synapses.
source: Pulido et al., 2015 investigated so called simple synapses where the synaptic connection is mediated by a single presynaptic AZ and the opposing PSD. Their results revealed that the number (N) of functional release sites (RSs) varied from 1 to 6 per AZ, and it showed a positive correlation with the quantal size (q).
evidence: This claim is based on results from a cited study by Pulido et al., 2015.

claim: In cerebellar molecular layer interneuron synapses, the number of functional release sites showed a positive correlation with the quantal size.
source: Their results revealed that the number (N) of functional release sites (RSs) varied from 1 to 6 per AZ, and it showed a positive correlation with the quantal size (q).
evidence: This claim is based on results from a cited study by Pulido et al., 2015.

claim: The GABAA receptor number scales linearly with the synapse area.
source: Because in these synapses q is largely determined by the number of postsynaptic GABAA receptors and because the GABAA receptor number scales linearly with the synapse area (Nusser et al., 1997), they concluded that the N linearly scales with the synaptic area.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nusser et al., 1997.

claim: The probability with which release occurs from a CA3 PC axon terminal correlates with the size of the synapse.
source: Previous results from our laboratory showed that the probability with which release occurs (PR) from a CA3 PC axon terminal correlates with the size of the synapse.
evidence: This claim references previous results from the authors' laboratory.

claim: The number of Munc13-1 macromolecular clusters shows a linear correlation with N and no correlation with Pv in cultured hippocampal neurons.
source: This view was further supported by a recent paper (Sakamoto et al., 2018), which concluded that in synapses of cultured hippocampal neurons the number of Munc13-1 macromolecular clusters shows a linear correlation with the N and no correlation with Pv.
evidence: This claim is based on conclusions from a cited study by Sakamoto et al., 2018.

claim: Munc13-1 and its invertebrate homologs are essential for docking and priming of synaptic vesicles.
source: Since Munc13-1 and its invertebrate homologs are essential for docking and priming of synaptic vesicles (Augustin et al., 1999; Imig et al., 2014; Weimer et al., 2006) and the fact that its cluster numbers show tight correlation with N suggests that it is a key molecule of the RSs and can be used as its molecular marker.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: Munc13-1 is a key molecule of release sites and can be used as its molecular marker.
source: Since Munc13-1 and its invertebrate homologs are essential for docking and priming of synaptic vesicles (Augustin et al., 1999; Imig et al., 2014; Weimer et al., 2006) and the fact that its cluster numbers show tight correlation with N suggests that it is a key molecule of the RSs and can be used as its molecular marker.
evidence: This is inferred from the essential role of Munc13-1 in vesicle docking/priming and its correlation with N.

claim: The number of presynaptic active zone molecules scales linearly with the synapse area.
source: This model is supported by a number of molecular neuroanatomical studies showing that the number of presynaptic AZ molecules (e.g. Cav2.1, Cav2.2, Rim1/2; Holderith et al., 2012; Kleindienst et al., 2020; Miki et al., 2017) or postsynaptic molecules (e.g. PSD-95, AMPA receptors; Fukazawa and Shigemoto, 2012; Kleindienst et al., 2020) scales linearly with the synapse area.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: The number of postsynaptic molecules scales linearly with the synapse area.
source: This model is supported by a number of molecular neuroanatomical studies showing that the number of presynaptic AZ molecules (e.g. Cav2.1, Cav2.2, Rim1/2; Holderith et al., 2012; Kleindienst et al., 2020; Miki et al., 2017) or postsynaptic molecules (e.g. PSD-95, AMPA receptors; Fukazawa and Shigemoto, 2012; Kleindienst et al., 2020) scales linearly with the synapse area.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies.

claim: Each release site faces a cluster of postsynaptic AMPA receptors in a nanocolumn arrangement.
source: Furthermore, it was also suggested that each RS faces a cluster of postsynaptic AMPA receptors in a so called nanocolumn arrangement (Tang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is based on a suggestion from a cited study by Tang et al., 2016.

claim: Release sites with high or low Pv are distributed in a nonrandom fashion within individual active zones.
source: However, a recent study using superresolution imaging of release from cultured neurons concluded that the RSs are functionally heterogeneous and RSs with high or low Pv are distributed in a nonrandom fashion within individual AZs (Maschi and Klyachko, 2020).
evidence: This claim is based on conclusions from a cited study by Maschi and Klyachko, 2020.

claim: The amplitude of unitary EPSCs evoked by CA1 PCs in FSINs ranged from 3 to 507 pA with a mean of 105.0 pA and a SD of 107.9 pA.
source: The amplitude of uEPSCs ranged from 3 to 507 pA with a mean of 105.0 pA and a SD of 107.9 pA, yielding a coefficient of variation (CV) of 1.03.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental measurements from paired recordings.

claim: The coefficient of variation of unitary EPSC amplitudes was 1.03.
source: The amplitude of uEPSCs ranged from 3 to 507 pA with a mean of 105.0 pA and a SD of 107.9 pA, yielding a coefficient of variation (CV) of 1.03.
evidence: This is calculated from experimental measurements.

claim: Unitary EPSCs had a moderate variability in their 10–90% rise times with a mean of 0.4 ± 0.2 ms and CV of 0.4.
source: The uEPSCs had a moderate variability in their 10–90% rise times (RT, mean = 0.4 ± 0.2 ms, CV = 0.4), but some had values over 1 ms.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental measurements.

claim: Fast-rising EPSCs (10-90% rise time ≤ 500 µs) had a mean amplitude of 113.1 ± 111.0 pA with a CV of 0.98.
source: These fast-rising EPSCs had a similar large variability in their amplitudes (113.1 ± 111.0 pA, n = 68; Figure 1D), with a CV of 0.98.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental measurements from a subselected population.

claim: Most PC-FSIN connections showed robust depression in short-term plasticity.
source: Although some connections displayed initial facilitation followed by depression, most of the connections showed robust depression, and the resulting moderate variability in the paired-pulse ratio (CV = 0.38; Figure 1E) implies that the variability in Pv might not be the major source of variability in EPSC amplitudes.
evidence: This is based on observations from paired recording experiments.

claim: The paired-pulse ratio showed moderate variability with a CV of 0.38.
source: Although some connections displayed initial facilitation followed by depression, most of the connections showed robust depression, and the resulting moderate variability in the paired-pulse ratio (CV = 0.38; Figure 1E) implies that the variability in Pv might not be the major source of variability in EPSC amplitudes.
evidence: This is calculated from experimental measurements.

claim: Variability in Pv might not be the major source of variability in EPSC amplitudes.
source: Although some connections displayed initial facilitation followed by depression, most of the connections showed robust depression, and the resulting moderate variability in the paired-pulse ratio (CV = 0.38; Figure 1E) implies that the variability in Pv might not be the major source of variability in EPSC amplitudes.
evidence: This is inferred from the moderate variability in paired-pulse ratio.

claim: No significant difference was found in uEPSC amplitudes between perisomatic region-targeting and bistratified FSINs.
source: A total of 50 FSINs could be categorized into perisomatic region-targeting (n = 35) or bistratified (n = 15) cells, and when uEPSCs amplitudes were compared (perisomatic: 128.1 ± 121.9 pA vs bistratified: 126.4 ± 125.7 pA), no significant difference was found (p=0.98, Mann–Whitney U-test).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of experimental data.

claim: The CV of EPSC peak amplitudes within perisomatic region-targeting FSINs was approximately 1.
source: Furthermore, the CV within each group was ~1, revealing a similar variance in EPSC peak amplitudes when the postsynaptic cells belong to a well-defined IN category.
evidence: This is calculated from experimental measurements within a subgroup.

claim: The CV of EPSC peak amplitudes within bistratified FSINs was approximately 1.
source: Furthermore, the CV within each group was ~1, revealing a similar variance in EPSC peak amplitudes when the postsynaptic cells belong to a well-defined IN category.
evidence: This is calculated from experimental measurements within a subgroup.

claim: The peak amplitude of uEPSCs in 6 mM [Ca2+] was significantly higher (165.5 ± 169.3 pA) than in 2 mM extracellular [Ca2+].
source: The peak amplitude of uEPSCs in 6 mM [Ca2+] was significantly higher (165.5 ± 169.3 pA, n = 100; p=4.42 × 10−4, Mann–Whitney U-test) than in 2 mM extracellular [Ca2+] but showed similarly large variability (CV = 1.0).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of experimental data under different conditions.

claim: Rise time-subselected, presumably perisomatic uEPSCs had a mean amplitude of 183.4 ± 180.7 pA with a CV of 0.99 in 6 mM [Ca2+].
source: The RT-subselected, presumably perisomatic uEPSCs had a mean amplitude of 183.4 ± 180.7 pA (n = 81) with a CV of 0.99, confirming our results in 2 mM [Ca2+] that dendritically unfiltered EPSCs are also highly variable.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental measurements from a subselected population.

claim: In 47 PC-FSIN pairs, the mean number of release sites (N) was 9.9 ± 9.0 with a CV of 0.91.
source: Of these 81 pairs, we managed to reliably determine the quantal parameters (see Materials and methods) in 47 pairs (peak amplitude: 215.8 ± 211.2 pA, CV = 0.98; Figure 2A) and found large variability in N (9.9 ± 9.0, CV = 0.91; Figure 2B), a much smaller variance in q (32.4 ± 16.0 pA, CV = 0.49; Figure 2C) and an especially low variance in Pv (0.72 ± 0.1, CV = 0.14; Figure 2D).
evidence: This is derived from quantal analysis of experimental data.

claim: The mean quantal size (q) was 32.4 ± 16.0 pA with a CV of 0.49 in 47 PC-FSIN pairs.
source: Of these 81 pairs, we managed to reliably determine the quantal parameters (see Materials and methods) in 47 pairs (peak amplitude: 215.8 ± 211.2 pA, CV = 0.98; Figure 2A) and found large variability in N (9.9 ± 9.0, CV = 0.91; Figure 2B), a much smaller variance in q (32.4 ± 16.0 pA, CV = 0.49; Figure 2C) and an especially low variance in Pv (0.72 ± 0.1, CV = 0.14; Figure 2D).
evidence: This is derived from quantal analysis of experimental data.

claim: The mean vesicular release probability (Pv) was 0.72 ± 0.1 with a CV of 0.14 in 47 PC-FSIN pairs in 6 mM [Ca2+].
source: Of these 81 pairs, we managed to reliably determine the quantal parameters (see Materials and methods) in 47 pairs (peak amplitude: 215.8 ± 211.2 pA, CV = 0.98; Figure 2A) and found large variability in N (9.9 ± 9.0, CV = 0.91; Figure 2B), a much smaller variance in q (32.4 ± 16.0 pA, CV = 0.49; Figure 2C) and an especially low variance in Pv (0.72 ± 0.1, CV = 0.14; Figure 2D).
evidence: This is derived from quantal analysis of experimental data.

claim: Peak amplitude of uEPSCs correlated tightly with N (Spearman regression coefficient = 0.79).
source: Peak amplitude of uEPSCs correlated tightly with N (Spearman regression coefficient (rs) = 0.79; Figure 2E), less tightly with q (rs = 0.38; Figure 2F) and with Pv (rs = 0.36; Figure 2G), demonstrating that variability in N is the major determinant of the uEPSC amplitude variability.
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of experimental data.

claim: Peak amplitude of uEPSCs correlated less tightly with q (Spearman regression coefficient = 0.38).
source: Peak amplitude of uEPSCs correlated tightly with N (Spearman regression coefficient (rs) = 0.79; Figure 2E), less tightly with q (rs = 0.38; Figure 2F) and with Pv (rs = 0.36; Figure 2G), demonstrating that variability in N is the major determinant of the uEPSC amplitude variability.
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of experimental data.

claim: Peak amplitude of uEPSCs correlated with Pv (Spearman regression coefficient = 0.36).
source: Peak amplitude of uEPSCs correlated tightly with N (Spearman regression coefficient (rs) = 0.79; Figure 2E), less tightly with q (rs = 0.38; Figure 2F) and with Pv (rs = 0.36; Figure 2G), demonstrating that variability in N is the major determinant of the uEPSC amplitude variability.
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of experimental data.

claim: Variability in N is the major determinant of the uEPSC amplitude variability.
source: Peak amplitude of uEPSCs correlated tightly with N (Spearman regression coefficient (rs) = 0.79; Figure 2E), less tightly with q (rs = 0.38; Figure 2F) and with Pv (rs = 0.36; Figure 2G), demonstrating that variability in N is the major determinant of the uEPSC amplitude variability.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the correlation analysis showing N has the strongest correlation with amplitude.

claim: The Pv in 2 mM [Ca2+] was smaller (mean = 0.42 ± 0.15) and more variable (CV = 0.36) compared to 6 mM [Ca2+] (mean = 0.71 ± 0.10, CV = 0.14).
source: As expected, the Pv was smaller (mean = 0.42 ± 0.15, n = 14) and more variable (CV = 0.36) in 2 mM [Ca2+] when compared to that in 6 mM [Ca2+] (mean = 0.71 ± 0.10, CV = 0.14, n = 14).
evidence: This is based on comparison of experimental measurements under different conditions.

claim: In 2 mM [Ca2+], the variance in N (63%) has a substantially larger contribution to amplitude variance than that of q (25%) or Pv (12%).
source: Because Pv in 2 mM [Ca2+] shows a more pronounced correlation with the peak EPSC amplitude (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), we calculated the relative contribution of the three quantal parameters to the amplitude variance and found that even in 2 mM [Ca2+], the variance in N (63%) has a substantially larger contribution than that of q (25%) or Pv (12%; for CV values in 2 mM [Ca2+], see Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is calculated from analysis of experimental data.

claim: There was a relatively weak correlation between peak uEPSC amplitude and the N/AZ (rs = 0.37).
source: Our data revealed a relatively weak correlation between peak uEPSC amplitude and the N/AZ (rs = 0.37; Figure 2H) and a more robust one between the peak uEPSC amplitude and the synapse number (rs = 0.61; Figure 2I).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of experimental data.

claim: There was a more robust correlation between peak uEPSC amplitude and the synapse number (rs = 0.61).
source: Our data revealed a relatively weak correlation between peak uEPSC amplitude and the N/AZ (rs = 0.37; Figure 2H) and a more robust one between the peak uEPSC amplitude and the synapse number (rs = 0.61; Figure 2I).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of experimental data.

claim: The mean number of synaptic contacts per connection was 2.3 ± 1.6 with a CV of 0.68.
source: When we examined their variances, an approximately equal contribution of the synapse number (mean = 2.3 ± 1.6, n = 26, CV = 0.68) and the N/AZ (mean = 4.9 ± 3.7, n = 26, CV = 0.75) to the variance in N (mean = 10.2 ± 9.8, n = 26, CV = 0.96) was observed.
evidence: This is derived from anatomical analysis of recorded cell pairs.

claim: The mean N/AZ was 4.9 ± 3.7 with a CV of 0.75.
source: When we examined their variances, an approximately equal contribution of the synapse number (mean = 2.3 ± 1.6, n = 26, CV = 0.68) and the N/AZ (mean = 4.9 ± 3.7, n = 26, CV = 0.75) to the variance in N (mean = 10.2 ± 9.8, n = 26, CV = 0.96) was observed.
evidence: This is derived from combining functional and anatomical data.

claim: There is approximately equal contribution of synapse number and N/AZ to the variance in N.
source: When we examined their variances, an approximately equal contribution of the synapse number (mean = 2.3 ± 1.6, n = 26, CV = 0.68) and the N/AZ (mean = 4.9 ± 3.7, n = 26, CV = 0.75) to the variance in N (mean = 10.2 ± 9.8, n = 26, CV = 0.96) was observed.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the CV values of synapse number and N/AZ.

claim: The summed immunoreactivity for Munc13-1 showed a significant positive correlation with the number of contacts per connection.
source: The summed immunoreactivity for Munc13-1 showed a significant positive correlation with the number of contacts per connection (Figure 3J, left panel).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of immunolabeling data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: A significant positive correlation (rs = 0.57) was found between Munc13-1 immunoreactivity and N/AZ.
source: When the correlations between the Munc13-1 immunoreactivity and N/AZ was examined, a significant positive correlation was found (rs = 0.57; Figure 3J, middle panel), but no significant correlation was observed between the Munc13-1 immunoreactivity and the Pv (rs = 0.02; Figure 3J, right panel).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of combined functional and molecular data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: No significant correlation was observed between Munc13-1 immunoreactivity and Pv (rs = 0.02).
source: When the correlations between the Munc13-1 immunoreactivity and N/AZ was examined, a significant positive correlation was found (rs = 0.57; Figure 3J, middle panel), but no significant correlation was observed between the Munc13-1 immunoreactivity and the Pv (rs = 0.02; Figure 3J, right panel).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of combined functional and molecular data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Synapses with widely different N/AZ had similar amounts of Munc13-1.
source: Although our results revealed positive correlations for both values with Munc13-1 (Figure 3J), we noticed a remarkable variability: synapses with widely different N/AZ had similar amounts of Munc13-1 and synapses with similar N/AZ showed very different amounts of Munc13-1 (Figure 3J).
evidence: This observation is based on visual inspection and analysis of data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Synapses with similar N/AZ showed very different amounts of Munc13-1.
source: Although our results revealed positive correlations for both values with Munc13-1 (Figure 3J), we noticed a remarkable variability: synapses with widely different N/AZ had similar amounts of Munc13-1 and synapses with similar N/AZ showed very different amounts of Munc13-1 (Figure 3J).
evidence: This observation is based on visual inspection and analysis of data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: The observed variance indicates variability in the overall amounts of Munc13-1 in individual release sites.
source: In summary, our data are consistent with a model in which the size of the presynaptic AZ correlates with the N/AZ, but the observed variance indicates variability in the overall amounts of Munc13-1 in individual RSs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed variability in Munc13-1 content among synapses with similar N/AZ.

claim: Active zones fractured on Kv3.1b+ interneuron somata and proximal dendrites are highly variable in size with a mean of 0.071 ± 0.014 µm² and CV of 0.43 ± 0.06.
source: AZs fractured on these Kv3.1b + IN somata and proximal dendrites are highly variable in size (mean = 0.071 ± 0.014 µm2, CV = 0.43 ± 0.06, n = 4 reactions in three mice) and contain variable number of gold particles labeling Munc13-1 (mean = 26.0 ± 5.1 gold, CV = 0.49 ± 0.08, n = 4; Figure 4C–G).
evidence: This is based on measurements from SDS-FRL experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Active zones on Kv3.1b+ interneurons contain variable number of gold particles labeling Munc13-1 with a mean of 26.0 ± 5.1 gold and CV of 0.49 ± 0.08.
source: AZs fractured on these Kv3.1b + IN somata and proximal dendrites are highly variable in size (mean = 0.071 ± 0.014 µm2, CV = 0.43 ± 0.06, n = 4 reactions in three mice) and contain variable number of gold particles labeling Munc13-1 (mean = 26.0 ± 5.1 gold, CV = 0.49 ± 0.08, n = 4; Figure 4C–G).
evidence: This is based on measurements from SDS-FRL experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: A significant positive correlation was observed between the active zone size and the Munc13-1 gold number.
source: Visual inspection of the EM images revealed that large AZs had many gold particles and small ones had fewer. Indeed, a significant positive correlation was observed between the AZ size and the Munc13-1 gold number in four experiments of three mice (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of SDS-FRL data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Munc13-1 density showed substantial variability (mean CV = 0.33 ± 0.07) and was slightly synapse size-dependent.
source: Plots showing the Munc13-1 density vs. the AZ area revealed substantial (mean CV = 0.33 ± 0.07) and slightly synapse size-dependent variability (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is based on analysis of SDS-FRL data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: Synapses with identical size could have a 10-fold difference in their Munc13-1 content.
source: Synapses with identical size could have a 10-fold difference in their Munc13-1 content, suggesting large variability in either the RS density or the amounts of Munc13-1 per RS.
evidence: This observation is based on analysis of SDS-FRL data.

claim: The number of gold particles for PSD-95 showed an extremely tight, positive correlation with the synapse area (rs = 0.96).
source: The number of gold particles for PSD-95 showed an extremely tight, positive correlation with the synapse area (rs = 0.96), resulting in a size-independent uniform PSD-95 density (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of SDS-FRL data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: PSD-95 density is size-independent and uniform.
source: The number of gold particles for PSD-95 showed an extremely tight, positive correlation with the synapse area (rs = 0.96), resulting in a size-independent uniform PSD-95 density (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is inferred from the tight correlation between PSD-95 gold number and synapse area shown in Figure 5.

claim: The variability in PSD-95 density was exceptionally small with a CV of 0.09.
source: The exceptionally small variability in the PSD-95 density (CV = 0.09) demonstrates the capability of SDS-FRL method to reveal uniform densities of synaptic molecules with a small variance.
evidence: This is calculated from SDS-FRL measurements.

claim: The variability in Munc13-1 density (CV = 0.33 ± 0.07) is substantially higher than PSD-95 density variability.
source: Because the variability in Munc13-1 density is substantially higher (CV = 0.33 ± 0.07) with similar mean values (Munc13-1: 383 ± 71 gold/µm2 vs PSD-95 in dendrites: 497 ± 45 gold/µm2) and because we demonstrate that this cannot be the consequence of a lower labeling efficiency of our Munc13-1 Ab (see Materials and methods), we concluded that the observed synapse to synapse variation in the Munc13-1 density must have a biological origin.
evidence: This is based on comparison of CV values from SDS-FRL measurements.

claim: The observed synapse to synapse variation in the Munc13-1 density must have a biological origin.
source: Because the variability in Munc13-1 density is substantially higher (CV = 0.33 ± 0.07) with similar mean values (Munc13-1: 383 ± 71 gold/µm2 vs PSD-95 in dendrites: 497 ± 45 gold/µm2) and because we demonstrate that this cannot be the consequence of a lower labeling efficiency of our Munc13-1 Ab (see Materials and methods), we concluded that the observed synapse to synapse variation in the Munc13-1 density must have a biological origin.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from comparing Munc13-1 and PSD-95 variability and ruling out technical sources.

claim: The mean nearest-neighbor distances between gold particles in active zones were significantly smaller than those of randomly distributed gold particles.
source: The mean NND distances were significantly smaller than those of randomly distributed gold particles (data: 0.026 ± 0.01 µm, random: 0.033 ± 0.009 µm, n = 159, p<0.001, Wilcoxon signed-rank test; Figure 4K).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of measured and simulated data shown in Figure 4K.

claim: In 66% of the active zones, the distribution of gold particles was compatible with clustering.
source: We performed this analysis on 159 AZs and found that in 66% of the AZs the distribution of gold particles was compatible with clustering (p<0.05, MAD test).
evidence: This is based on Ripley's H-function analysis of SDS-FRL data.

claim: The mean number of Munc13-1 clusters per active zone was 5.4 ± 2.5 using DBSCAN analysis with ε = 31 nm and MinPts = 2.
source: We then determined the mean number of clusters (Nc = 5.4 ± 2.5) with this ε value and a MinPts of 2.
evidence: This is derived from DBSCAN cluster analysis of SDS-FRL data.

claim: The average of ~5 clusters per active zone is remarkably similar to the N/AZ (4.9 ± 3.7).
source: The average of ~5 clusters per AZ is remarkably similar to the N/AZ (4.9 ± 3.7), supporting the notion that Munc13-1 clusters are indeed the molecular equivalents of the functional RSs (Sakamoto et al., 2018).
evidence: This comparison is made between cluster analysis results and functional measurements.

claim: Munc13-1 clusters are the molecular equivalents of the functional release sites.
source: The average of ~5 clusters per AZ is remarkably similar to the N/AZ (4.9 ± 3.7), supporting the notion that Munc13-1 clusters are indeed the molecular equivalents of the functional RSs (Sakamoto et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity between cluster number and N/AZ, and supported by citation.

claim: A significant positive correlation was found between the number of Munc13-1 clusters and active zone area.
source: When the number of clusters were plotted against the AZ area, a significant positive correlation was found (Figure 4L).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of cluster data shown in Figure 4L.

claim: The number of Munc13-1 clusters varied fourfold in synapses of identical sizes, resulting in a CV of 0.36 in cluster density.
source: However, the number of clusters also varied fourfold in synapses of identical sizes, resulting in a CV of 0.36 in the cluster density (mean: 73 ± 27 clusters/µm2 AZ area, n = 105).
evidence: This is based on analysis of cluster density data from SDS-FRL.

claim: The Munc13-1 content of clusters is highly variable (4.5 ± 3.0 gold/cluster, CV = 0.67).
source: We also noticed that not only the cluster density varies, but the Munc13-1 content of the clusters (4.5 ± 3.0 gold/cluster, CV = 0.67, n = 571) is also highly variable (for individual AZs see Figure 4H).
evidence: This is based on measurements of gold particles per cluster from SDS-FRL data.

claim: The mean nearest-neighbor inter-cluster distance was 85 ± 34 nm.
source: Finally, we measured the nearest-neighbor inter-cluster distance and obtained a mean of 85 ± 34 nm (n = 568 distances from 102 AZs) that is consistent with the spacing and size of docked synaptic vesicles.
evidence: This is based on measurements from SDS-FRL data.

claim: The mean nearest-neighbor inter-cluster distance is consistent with the spacing and size of docked synaptic vesicles.
source: Finally, we measured the nearest-neighbor inter-cluster distance and obtained a mean of 85 ± 34 nm (n = 568 distances from 102 AZs) that is consistent with the spacing and size of docked synaptic vesicles.
evidence: This is inferred by comparing the measured distance to known vesicle dimensions.

claim: Relative Munc13-1 and PSD-95 intensities showed a loose correlation in two examined cells.
source: In the two examined cells relative Munc13-1 and PSD-95 intensities showed a loose correlation (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of STED imaging data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The PSD-95 normalized Munc13-1 labeling showed substantial variability (Cell 1: CV = 0.42; Cell 2: CV = 0.40) in 200 nm sections.
source: More importantly, the PSD-95 normalized Munc13-1 labeling showed a substantial variability (Cell 1: CV = 0.42; Cell 2: CV = 0.40) and a slight synapse size- (PSD-95 intensity) dependence, like that obtained with SDS-FRL (compare Figure 4J with Figure 6E).
evidence: This is calculated from quantitative analysis of STED imaging data.

claim: The PSD-95 normalized Munc13-1 signal showed large variability (CV = 0.40) in 70 nm sections with 3D reconstruction.
source: As can be seen in the superimposed STED images in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, the relative proportion of cyan (Munc13-1) and red (PSD-95) signals varies substantially, resulting in a large variability in the PSD-95 normalized Munc13-1 signal (CV = 0.40, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D,E) again consistent with our SDS-FRL results and indicating that the different amounts of Munc13-1 in synapses with identical N/AZ are likely to be of biological origin.
evidence: This is calculated from quantitative analysis of STED imaging data with 3D reconstruction.

claim: The different amounts of Munc13-1 in synapses with identical N/AZ are likely to be of biological origin.
source: As can be seen in the superimposed STED images in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, the relative proportion of cyan (Munc13-1) and red (PSD-95) signals varies substantially, resulting in a large variability in the PSD-95 normalized Munc13-1 signal (CV = 0.40, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D,E) again consistent with our SDS-FRL results and indicating that the different amounts of Munc13-1 in synapses with identical N/AZ are likely to be of biological origin.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from consistency between STED and SDS-FRL results.

claim: PC to FS basket cell synaptic connections are mediated by a remarkably similar number of synapses across species (mean ~3, range 1-7).
source: PC to FS basket cell synaptic connections are mediated by a remarkably similar number of synapses in human neocortex (mean = 3.3, range: 1–6; Molnár et al., 2016), cat visual cortex (mean = 3.4, range: 1–7; Buhl et al., 1997), rat neocortex (mean = 2.9, range 1–6; Molnár et al., 2016), and mouse hippocampus (mean = 2.3, range: 1–7; present study).
evidence: This comparison is made across multiple cited studies and the present study.

claim: The multi-synapse connection between pyramidal cells and GABAergic local circuit interneurons is an evolutionary conserved feature of cortical networks.
source: All data taken together demonstrate that the multi-synapse connection between PCs and GABAergic local circuit INs is an evolutionary conserved feature of cortical networks.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the similarity in synapse numbers across multiple species.

claim: N/AZ was approximately 4 times larger in human (~6) compared to rat (1.6) cortical PC-FSIN connections.
source: Molnár et al., 2016 reported that the N/AZ was ~4 times larger in human (~6) compared to rat (1.6) cortical PC–FSIN connections.
evidence: This is based on data from a cited study by Molnár et al., 2016.

claim: N/AZ in adult mouse hippocampus (4.9) is very similar to that found in mouse cultured hippocampal neurons.
source: It is 4.9 for the same connection in adult mouse hippocampus, which is very similar to that found in mouse cultured hippocampal neurons (4.9 in Sakamoto et al., 2018 and 4.2 in Ariel et al., 2012; but 8.7 in Maschi and Klyachko, 2017).
evidence: This comparison is made between the present study and cited studies.

claim: The active zone size in human (0.077 µm²) is similar to that in adult mice (0.071 µm²).
source: The difference in N/AZ between human and rat was accompanied by a larger AZ size in human (0.077 µm2), which is again similar to that obtained in our present study in adult mice (0.071 µm2), indicating that both in human and mice a RS occupies (or needs) approximately the same AZ area.
evidence: This comparison is made between cited data and the present study.

claim: Both in human and mice, a release site occupies approximately the same active zone area.
source: The difference in N/AZ between human and rat was accompanied by a larger AZ size in human (0.077 µm2), which is again similar to that obtained in our present study in adult mice (0.071 µm2), indicating that both in human and mice a RS occupies (or needs) approximately the same AZ area.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity in AZ size and N/AZ between human and mice.

claim: There is large variability in the number of docked vesicles in active zones with identical sizes.
source: First, there is large variability in the number of docked vesicles in AZs with identical sizes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 in Molnár et al., 2016), which might reflect variability in RS density, but an incomplete docking site/RS occupancy cannot be excluded.
evidence: This observation is based on data from a cited study.

claim: Active zones with the same amount of PSD-95 have >3 fold variability in N.
source: Such incomplete RS occupancy cannot explain our data showing that AZs with the same amount of PSD-95 (same size) have >3 fold variability in N.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the present study's data.

claim: The actual release site density appears to be variable.
source: Thus, it seems that variability in the docking site occupancy might not be the main source of variability, but the actual RS density seem to be variable.
evidence: This is inferred from ruling out docking site occupancy as the main source of variability.

claim: The almost identical number of release sites and readily releasable pool size indicates a docking site occupancy close to one in cultured hippocampal neurons.
source: The almost identical number of RSs and NRRP indicates a docking site occupancy close to one in their cultured hippocampal neurons again arguing for the variability in either the RS density or in the number of Munc13-1 molecules per RS.
evidence: This is inferred from data in a cited study by Sakamoto et al., 2018.

claim: The average Pv of release sites does not depend on the N/AZ.
source: Our data, showing that the average Pv of the RSs does not depend on the N/AZ (Figure 2J), together with that of Sakamoto et al., 2018, demonstrating that Pv does not depend on the NRRP, strongly indicate that the average Pv does not depend on the size of AZ.
evidence: This is based on analysis of data shown in Figure 2J and comparison with cited study.

claim: The average Pv does not depend on the size of active zone.
source: Our data, showing that the average Pv of the RSs does not depend on the N/AZ (Figure 2J), together with that of Sakamoto et al., 2018, demonstrating that Pv does not depend on the NRRP, strongly indicate that the average Pv does not depend on the size of AZ.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of correlation between Pv and N/AZ or NRRP.

claim: The probability with which release occurs at hippocampal synapses depends on the active zone size.
source: A pervious study from our laboratory (Holderith et al., 2012) described that the probability with which release occurs at hippocampal synapses (PR) depends on the AZ size.
evidence: This is based on results from a cited study by the authors' laboratory.

claim: The synapse size-dependent increase in N fully explains the relationship between PR and synapse size.
source: We would like to stress that this probability (PR) is the function of both the Pv and N [PR = 1-(1-Pv)N]; therefore, the synapse size-dependent increase in N fully explains our previous and current results.
evidence: This is inferred from the mathematical relationship between PR, Pv, and N.

claim: Munc13-1 is an evolutionally conserved presynaptic protein that is essential for docking and priming vesicles for release.
source: Munc13-1 is an evolutionally conserved presynaptic protein that is essential for docking and priming vesicles for release (Augustin et al., 1999; Betz et al., 2001; Brockmann et al., 2020; Imig et al., 2014; Jahn and Fasshauer, 2012; Ma et al., 2011; Varoqueaux et al., 2002); therefore, it can be hypothesized that the amount of this molecule might have an effect on the docking site occupancy or the priming state of the vesicles.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: The amount of Munc13-1 might have an effect on the docking site occupancy or the priming state of vesicles.
source: Munc13-1 is an evolutionally conserved presynaptic protein that is essential for docking and priming vesicles for release (Augustin et al., 1999; Betz et al., 2001; Brockmann et al., 2020; Imig et al., 2014; Jahn and Fasshauer, 2012; Ma et al., 2011; Varoqueaux et al., 2002); therefore, it can be hypothesized that the amount of this molecule might have an effect on the docking site occupancy or the priming state of the vesicles.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the known function of Munc13-1.

claim: Pocc is high (~0.8) at neocortical/hippocampal glutamatergic synapses.
source: As mentioned above, Sakamoto et al., 2018 came to this conclusion from the similar NRRP and Molnár et al., 2016 examined the number of docked vesicles at cortical PC–FSIN synapses and determined N, and found rather similar values for both human and rat synapses, arguing for a Pocc of ~0.8 that is similar to that found at the Calyx of Held (Neher, 2010), but larger than at cerebellar IN synapses (Pulido et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from cited studies comparing docked vesicles and N.

claim: Variability in Pocc might not be the major consequence of the variable amounts of Munc13-1 per release site.
source: Thus, it seems that variability in Pocc might not be the major consequence of the variable amounts of Munc13-1 per RS, indicating that the priming state of the vesicles and therefore the Psucc might be affected.
evidence: This is inferred from the evidence that Pocc is high and relatively uniform.

claim: The priming state of vesicles and therefore Psucc might be affected by variable amounts of Munc13-1.
source: Thus, it seems that variability in Pocc might not be the major consequence of the variable amounts of Munc13-1 per RS, indicating that the priming state of the vesicles and therefore the Psucc might be affected.
evidence: This is speculated based on ruling out Pocc as the major variable.

claim: Heterogeneity in Pv for different vesicles has been demonstrated at the active zones of the Calyx of Held.
source: Heterogeneity in the Pv for different vesicles has been demonstrated at the AZs of the Calyx of Held (reviewed by Neher, 2017).
evidence: This is based on a cited review.

claim: At the Calyx of Held, approximately half of the vesicles have high Pv and the other half have low Pv.
source: Here, approximately half of the vesicles have high and the other halves have low Pv.
evidence: This is based on cited literature about the Calyx of Held.

claim: There is heterogeneity in the Pv of fast releasing vesicles (normally primed and superprimed vesicles) in the Calyx and hippocampal synapses.
source: Furthermore, there is also data indicating further heterogeneity in the Pv of the fast releasing (high Pv) vesicles in the Calyx (normally primed and superprimed vesicles; Taschenberger et al., 2016 and in hippocampal synapses as well Hanse and Gustafsson, 2001; Schlüter et al., 2006).
evidence: This is based on cited studies.

claim: The priming efficacy of Munc13-1 depends on its interaction with RIM and RIM binding protein.
source: It is noteworthy that the priming efficacy of Munc13-1 depends on its interaction with RIM and RIM binding protein (Brockmann et al., 2020) therefore predicting the functional consequence of the different amounts of Munc13-1 per RS might require the determination of these molecules in individual Munc13-1 clusters.
evidence: This is based on a cited study by Brockmann et al., 2020.

claim: The Pv of centrally located release sites is higher and they participate more frequently in multivesicular release than peripherally located release sites.
source: Maschi and Klyachko, 2020 demonstrated that the Pv of centrally located RSs is higher and participate more frequently in multivesicular release (MVR) than those that are located at the periphery of the AZs.
evidence: This is based on results from a cited study by Maschi and Klyachko, 2020.

claim: The number of RIM1 clusters in the active zone was similar to that of PSD-95 in the postsynaptic density and they face one another.
source: Specifically, the number of RIM1 clusters in the AZ was similar to that of PSD-95 in the PSD and they face one another in a remarkable fashion.
evidence: This is based on results from a cited study by Tang et al., 2016.

claim: Postsynaptic AMPA receptors do not show clustered sub-synaptic distribution in cerebellar and hippocampal glutamatergic synapses on GABAergic interneurons.
source: A more direct evidence against the nanocolumn organization as a universal feature of all glutamatergic synapses comes from a previous study form our laboratory, demonstrating that postsynaptic AMPA receptors do not show clustered sub-synaptic distribution in cerebellar and hippocampal glutamatergic synapses on GABAergic INs (Szoboszlay et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on results from a cited study by the authors' laboratory.

claim: The nanocolumn arrangement of pre- and postsynaptic key signaling molecules is not a universal feature of all glutamatergic synapses.
source: All these data taken together indicates that the nanocolumn arrangement of pre- and postsynaptic key signaling molecules is not a universal feature of all glutamatergic synapses.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from multiple lines of evidence including the present study and cited studies.

claim: Individual cortical synapses can release more than a single vesicle from an active zone upon the arrival of a single action potential.
source: Our results are also compatible with the concept that individual cortical synapses release more than a single vesicle from an AZ upon the arrival of a single AP (called MVR; Biró et al., 2006; Christie, 2006; Maschi and Klyachko, 2020; Pulido et al., 2015; Rudolph et al., 2015; Wadiche and Jahr, 2001).
evidence: This is consistent with the concept of multivesicular release supported by multiple citations.

claim: The occurrence of multivesicular release is the function of N/AZ and Pv.
source: The occurrence of MVR is the function of N/AZ and Pv.
evidence: This is based on the definition and understanding of multivesicular release.

claim: Cortical/hippocampal excitatory and inhibitory synaptic active zones contain multiple release sites, the number of which positively correlates with the size of the active zone.
source: All available data indicate that cortical/hippocampal excitatory and inhibitory synaptic AZs contain multiple RSs, the number of which positively correlates with the size of the AZ, fulfilling one essential requirement of MVR.
evidence: This is based on the present study's data and cited literature.

claim: Pv at hippocampal CA1 PC to O-LM cell synapses is so low that the occurrence of multivesicular release is negligible under physiological conditions.
source: A previous study from our laboratory demonstrated that Pv at hippocampal CA1 PC to O-LM cell synapses is so low that the occurrence of MVR is negligible under physiological conditions (Biró et al., 2005).
evidence: This is based on results from a cited study by the authors' laboratory.

claim: The Pv at PC-FSIN synapses is an order of magnitude higher (~0.4) than that at PC-O-LM synapses.
source: However, the Pv at PC–FSIN synapses is an order of magnitude higher (~0.4) than that at PC–O-LM synapses and given an average of five RSs per AZ, the probability of MVR is around 70%.
evidence: This is based on comparison of data from the present study and cited study.

claim: Given an average of five release sites per active zone at PC-FSIN synapses, the probability of multivesicular release is around 70%.
source: However, the Pv at PC–FSIN synapses is an order of magnitude higher (~0.4) than that at PC–O-LM synapses and given an average of five RSs per AZ, the probability of MVR is around 70%.
evidence: This is calculated from the Pv and N/AZ values.

claim: Pv at CA3 to CA1 PC synapses is probably between PC-FSIN and PC-O-LM values, indicating that the occurrence of multivesicular release is much less prominent.
source: We would like to emphasize that Pv at CA3 to CA1 PC synapses is probably in between these values, indicating that the occurrence of MVR is much less prominent.
evidence: This is speculated based on comparison with other synapse types.

claim: If receptor occupancy is high, the effect of simultaneously released multiple vesicles is small.
source: If the occupancy is high (e.g. cerebellar climbing fiber to Purkinje cell synapses; Harrison and Jahr, 2003 or at cerebellar molecular layer IN synapses, Auger et al., 1998; Nusser et al., 1997), the effect of simultaneously released multiple vesicles is small (not necessarily zero, because of the effect on the time course of the postsynaptic response; Rudolph et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on cited studies and general understanding of receptor occupancy.

claim: Receptor occupancy is relatively low at most central glutamatergic synapses.
source: However, increasing evidence indicates that receptor occupancy is relatively low at most central glutamatergic synapses, allowing the postsynaptic cell to detect the number of simultaneously released vesicles within a single synapse either linearly or sublinearly.
evidence: This is based on increasing evidence in the field.

claim: There is no correlation between quantal size (q) and N/AZ.
source: Our result, showing no correlation between the q and N/AZ (Figure 2J), is also consistent with this.
evidence: This is based on analysis of data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Multivesicular release operation of synapses increases the reliability of transmission and reduces stochastic trial-to-trial variability.
source: Such MVR operation of synapses by increasing the reliability of transmission and reducing stochastic trial-to-trial variability might provide an important circuit element with which perisomatic GABAergic inhibition is recruited reliably by an active ensemble of PCs.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional consequence of MVR.
